China’s centralized wastewater treatment 
system reaches efficiency limits in tackling 
water scarcity
 
Jijie Shen 
  1,2,3,6, Lei Shen 
  1,2,3,6, Shuai Zhong

Centralized wastewater treatment systems (CWTSs) are increasingly 
expected to strengthen water security through reclaimed water reuse. Yet 
whether centralized expansion can simultaneously achieve cost recovery 
and reduce water stress remains unresolved. We assess the viability of 
CWTSs in China using an inventory of 10,826 wastewater treatment plants 
and data on wastewater generation, reuse demand and socioeconomic 
scenarios. Here we show that CWTS benefits are spatially bounded: only 
approximately 0.45 billion people live in areas where reclaimed water reuse 
can achieve cost recovery and reduce local water stress. Under prevailing 
fees of 0.9–1.1 Chinese yuan m−3, cost recovery requires plants to reach 
break-even scales of 6,793–49,744 m3 per day. Projected urbanization 
does not substantially expand viable reuse opportunities, leaving 95–99% 
of prospective plants in unserved areas below break-even scale. Hybrid 
centralized–decentralized systems can meet national targets at 25–37% 
lower cost. These findings support a transition from purely centralized to 
coordinated hybrid systems in developing regions.
Wastewater is increasingly viewed as a supplementary water source for 
easing pressure on conventional freshwater supplies1–5. Centralized 
wastewater treatment systems (CWTSs), which integrate wastewater 
collection, conveyance, treatment and reclaimed water production, 
have become a major route for non-potable water reuse6,7. Global waste-
water treatment service coverage increased from 31% in 2000 to 55% 
in 20208,9, improving pollutant removal10,11 and increasing reclaimed 
water supply12,13 through advanced treatment14,15. This expansion of 
wastewater treatment services has created new opportunities to use 
reclaimed water in water-scarce regions12,16. Yet the expansion alone 
does not determine whether reclaimed water can effectively alleviate 
water scarcity.
Whether CWTSs effectively mitigate water scarcity depends on 
how well wastewater generation, treatment capacity, sewer access 
and reclaimed water demand are spatially aligned. It also depends 
on whether tariff revenues can cover system costs13,17–19. Population 
redistribution17,20, industrial restructuring21,22 and changing water-use 
patterns23,24 can shift wastewater loads and reuse demand away from 
existing infrastructure. At the same time, the high fixed costs of treat-
ment plants and sewer networks require sufficient utilization and stable 
revenue over the lifetime of CWTSs25. When these conditions become 
spatially misaligned, CWTSs may increase treated wastewater volumes 
without substantially improving local water security, and may remain 
technically functional while failing to recover costs26–28. Thus, the key 
question is not only how much wastewater can be treated but also where 
centralized reuse can replace enough freshwater and recover its costs.
